title: “So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?”: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India
shows: Human Rights Watch says in a 95-page report on India's institutions that the Election Commission faces what it calls a massive crisis of credibility. It says the revision begun in June 2025 had deleted over 130 million names by October 2026, in a process it describes as arbitrary and opaque, and that it disproportionately excluded women, people living in poverty, religious minorities, particularly Muslims, and other marginalised communities. It describes the rules as changing across three phases. In Bihar voters had to give one of 11 documents, in the second phase they had to trace themselves or a parent to the rolls of the 2002 to 2006 revisions and names were deleted for what the Commission called logical discrepancies, and in the third phase Form 6 was changed to ask whether an applicant's parents or grandparents were in the last revision, a change it says two election commissioners reportedly objected to. It says the Commission directed that electors deleted from the roll be enrolled again on Form 6, which in its account required them to declare falsely that they were applying for the first time. It says about 93 percent of the West Bengal electors whose appeals were decided were restored, that the Calcutta High Court said the over 3.4 million appeals still pending would take at least 21 years to resolve, and that information on deleted electors was used to halt passport renewals and to deny access to social security programmes and residence certificates for students. It finds that the Commission has failed to hold the Prime Minister and senior BJP leaders to account for apparent violations of the code of conduct and to investigate allegations of irregularities credibly, and that the law of December 2023 entrenched the executive's control over the appointment of election commissioners. It recommends that the revision be scrapped at once and that an independent investigation be set up into allegations of politically motivated interference. The report rests on more than 40 interviews held between January 2025 and September 2026 and on published sources.
quote: The commission is currently facing a massive crisis of credibility amid concerns over its ability to function independent of the executive.

Immediately scrap the Special Intensive Revision process, restore every citizen’s right to participate in elections, ensure that no one improperly loses access to social security and other programs, and establish an independent investigation into allegations of politically motivated interference.
note: First reading, 24 November 2026. The report's page on hrw.org, published 23 November 2026 at 8:30 pm EST (24 November in India), and the full report as a PDF linked from it (hrw.org/sites/default/files/media_2026/11/india1126web.pdf, 95 pages before the endnotes, dated November 2026, ISBN 979-8-88708-319-3) were read with curl on 24 November 2026, the PDF through pdftotext. The news release of the same day (hrw.org/news/2026/11/23/india-modi-rule-has-weakened-democratic-institutions) was also read, and the first quote is from it. The second quote is from the report's recommendations to the Government of India. The Wire's report of 24 November pointed to it and is not used. The summary covers only what the report says about the revision and the Commission, in its summary, its recommendations and the section on the Election Commission (pages 51 to 58). Every finding is Human Rights Watch's, including those on religion, and its interviewees are not named here. Set against data/india/states.json, the 'over 130 million names' it says were deleted by October 2026 are close to the names left off the drafts in 31 states, 13,39,03,307, which is more than 13 crore. Those names were left off the drafts, which is a different step from deletion by an order after a draft. The report does not draw that line, so its word deleted is given as its own. Its West Bengal figure of 'over nine million people, 12 percent of the electorate' matches no figure in states.json, which has 58,20,899 left off the draft, 5,46,053 deleted after it, 60,06,675 withheld and a fall in the roll of 1,21,84,920 from the roll before the revision to the final roll, and it is not carried. Its 'nearly 4.7 million' deleted in Bihar is close to Bihar's fall in the roll, 47,73,025, and is not carried. Its 93 percent of decided West Bengal appeals restored is the figure from the Times of India report of 21 September 2026 that Human Rights Watch's release of 28 October also cited, and it reads that figure as showing that 9 in 10 electors removed were wrongfully removed, a reading the summary does not carry. Its Patharpratima figure of over 92 percent Muslim among those deleted now cites a Sabar Institute factsheet on Google Drive and is not carried. The 3.4 million pending appeals and the 21 years are the Calcutta High Court's remark as Scroll reported it on 9 July 2026. The report's account of protests, of the court and of expulsions is outside the summary. Human Rights Watch's earlier release of 28 October 2026 on the revision is in round 29.

title: Maharashtra CEO Responds: Two Truths in Two Records
shows: This reply concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In a blog post of 24 November signed by its editors, the Reporters' Collective answers the letter of 20 November in which the office of Maharashtra's Chief Electoral Officer called misleading its report that the Commission has no record of how many citizens voted after 5 pm in the 2024 elections. The Collective says it stands by its reporting and that the Chief Electoral Officer has not disputed that the internal reports it cites exist or what they contain. It says all reports the Commission and its officials produce should reflect the same data, that the internal reports it read are prescribed by the Commission's manuals, are mandatory and are sent to the Commission in sealed envelopes, and that the manual says any difference between the count of voters who polled and the votes counted should be investigated as a case of potential rigging. It says the manual requires officials to record the voters and the votes polled every two hours until polling ends, and that filling in these figures after polling is over defeats the purpose of an audit. On the letter's complaint that questions sent at 10.03 am on 16 November asked for a reply by 5 pm that day, the Collective says it gave adequate time, that the office neither replied nor asked for more time, and that the questions needed no check of older records.
quote: There is no such thing as a ‘statutory truth’ and an ‘administrative truth’.
We stand by all assertions, evidence and facts in our reportage.
note: First reading, 24 November 2026. Read in full from the Collective's blog page with curl on 24 November 2026. The page prints 'Published on November 24, 2026' under the label Reality Check and 'From the Editor's Desk', its JSON-LD gives Nov 24, 2026, and the post is signed 'Editors, The Reporters' Collective.' with no names, so no author is given. Both quotes are verbatim. The post sets out lettered claims it attributes to the Chief Electoral Officer and answers them. Claim D ('Two hourly information mentioned in the RO report is only primary appropriate information') and claim H (on working out the votes after 5 pm by subtraction) match the letter's pages 2 and 3, read again as images on 24 November 2026. Claims A to C, on administrative and statutory reports, are the post's summary of the letter, which describes the returning officer's report as an administrative narrative and a non-statutory summary. Claims E and I are printed twice in the post with the same words. The post links the Collective's report of 18 November and the letter as posted on X. It concerns the 2024 polls, so nothing in it can be checked against the site's roll data, and every claim is the Collective's. The summary gives no view on which side is right. It is the Collective's answer to the Chief Electoral Officer's letter in round 52. The report it defends is in round 50, and the post is grouped under Investigations with it.
